roles.role: U.S. infantry company officer (captain, lieutenant, ensign) and surgeon's mate, August 1812

garments: Coat: dark blue wool, single-breasted, long skirts to the bend of the knee (longer than the private's), scarlet standing collar to the ear and scarlet cuffs, white turnbacks/lining, white-metal (silver) buttons, silver lace loops on the collar (and probably on the breast as in Pike's portrait); grade: inferred (Pike 1808 portrait shows blue/scarlet/silver; the 1813 change took away red collars and cuffs and lace, so they were there before; the Dec 1812 transcription to verify gives the full spec).

Epaulette: one silver bullion epaulette; captain on the right shoulder, lieutenant on the left (by analogy with the light artillery text printed 1814); ensign: reconstructed (none or as lieutenant; no source found).

Waistcoat white, single-breasted; breeches or pantaloons white (nankeen in summer per the staff text of 1813-14); black leather or silk stock; high boots: inferred from the staff/artillery text and Krimmel's officer.

Headwear: black felt chapeau bras (bicorne), black cockade about 4.5 in with an eagle, a white feather rising about 8 in, worn fore-and-aft as Krimmel's officer wears it: inferred by analogy (artillery text) and Krimmel.
Sash: crimson/red silk, worn round the waist and only on a tour of duty (artillery text); Krimmel shows officers with red/crimson sashes: inferred.

Sword: straight, yellow (brass/gilt) mounted with black or yellow grip (artillery: cut and thrust) on a white leather waist belt: inferred by analogy. Infantry officers' mounts may have been silver to match buttons: reconstructed.

Undress at a remote post in August (likely what a daily figure wears): the same coat, perhaps unbuttoned, round hat or chapeau, no sash, linen pantaloons: reconstruction; the 1813 change says 'The rules with respect to undress, are dispensed with, excepting that cockades must always be worn', showing an undress rule existed.

Surgeon's mate (Isaac Van Voorhis at Fort Dearborn): the regimental officer's coat but with a black velvet collar/cape and a black plume (artillery surgeons and mates, printed 1814); hospital surgeons and mates in black coats; the transcription to verify says medical staff wore blue collars and cuffs. Sources disagree; build blue coat with black velvet collar, chapeau with black plume, no sash, and record the liberty. He may well have worn civilian dress: reconstruction.
build.colours: coat dark indigo blue (as the private's coat_blue_1812); collar/cuffs scarlet brighter and cleaner than the private's (officer's superfine cloth); lace, buttons and epaulette silver (bright metal, not the private's pewter grey); waistcoat and breeches white; chapeau and stock black; sash crimson.
build.fit: Tailored close through the chest and waist, waist seam at natural waist or slightly above, skirts to the back of the knee; high collar to the ear; boots to the knee.

references.evidences: blue coat, scarlet laced collar and facings, silver lace, white buttons, silver epaulette, black stock on a U.S. infantry officer, 1808

roles.role: Sergeant, corporal and musician (drummer, fifer) of 1812 infantry

garments: Sergeant and corporal: the private's dress (coat, felt cap, overalls, crossbelts) with rank marks. Worsted epaulettes: sergeant two, corporal one on the right shoulder: inferred by analogy only (the rule printed in 1814 is for light dragoon NCOs: 'Sergeants to wear two white epaulettes, corporals one on the right shoulder'). For infantry the colour of the worsted (white or red) is not evidenced: reconstruction. Sergeants may carry a sword or halberd/spontoon rather than musket: not evidenced here; leave musket.

Musician: reversed colours, i.e. scarlet coat faced blue (collar, cuffs), white crossbelt or drum carriage, drum painted, same cap: directly shown for a Philadelphia volunteer drummer in Krimmel 1811-13; the regulars' red musicians' coats are claimed by the reenactor page only. Build as red faced blue, inferred.
Fifer: same coat, fife case on a shoulder belt in place of the cartridge box: reconstruction.
build.colours: musician coat scarlet with dark blue collar and cuffs; drum shell natural wood or painted, hoops red/blue: reconstructed; NCO epaulettes worsted white (reconstructed).

roles.role: Soldiers in fatigue dress at work (August)

garments: Fatigue frock: coarse unbleached linen, loose, pulled on over the head or open-fronted, thigh length: the issue 'one coarse linen frock and trowsers for fatigue clothing' is direct (1802 act; repeated in the act of January 1812); the cut is reconstruction.
Fatigue trousers: coarse linen, loose, full length, unbleached/off-white: direct issue, cut reconstructed.
Shirt (four a year) and stock may be worn without coat: direct issue; a man in shirt-sleeves and waistcoat ('vest') is equally supported.
Headwear: no fatigue cap is in the 1802 or 1812 issue; use the issued felt hat/cap left off, a civilian round hat, or bare head: reconstruction. Do NOT build a forage cap of a later pattern.
Shoes: issued black shoes, without gaiters.
build.colours: linen natural/oatmeal (lighter and greyer than the white overalls of dress); waistcoat white; shirt white/unbleached.
build.fit: Loose and long; sleeves rolled for work (reconstruction). Krimmel's Black Sawyers and Wayside Inn show how civilian working men of these years wore shirtsleeves, waistcoats and round hats, a cross-check for posture and looseness, not for army issue.

references.evidences: 'one coarse linen frock and trowsers for fatigue clothing' in the yearly issue (Sec. 8 of the 1802 act, p. 53; again Sec. 9 of the act of 11 January 1812)

roles.role: Officer's wife (Rebekah Heald, Margaret Helm) and enlisted man's wife / laundress

garments: Officer's wife: high-waisted (waist under the bust) gown of white or light cotton/muslin, long sleeves for day, ankle-length skirt with fullness at the back; a white cotton cap indoors; a close bonnet out of doors; a shawl (white cotton, or coloured); a short spencer jacket for cool mornings; flat slippers or half-boots. Grade: inferred. At Fort Dearborn itself Wau-Bun records Mrs. Heald's bonnet, 'shawls, ribbons, and feathers' and 'a muslin gown, and the bonnet of one of the ladies' plundered from the fort: direct for the materials present on 15 August 1812 (a later, family-transmitted narrative).

Enlisted man's wife / laundress: short gown (a loose hip-length jacket-bodice) and petticoat of printed cotton, linen or homespun, an apron, a kerchief at the neck, a cap or a cotton handkerchief tied round the head; bare arms for washing. Grade: inferred from Wau-Bun's 'ordinary dress of a French woman of the country; namely, a short gown and petticoat, with a blue cotton handkerchief wrapped around her head' (Chicago, August 1812), Lambert's 'petticoat and short jacket', and Krimmel's working woman in head-wrap, white bodice and striped petticoat.
No portrait of Rebekah Heald or Margaret Helm was found; any likeness is invention.
build.colours: gowns white/cream (fine), or printed cottons and coloured silks (blue, yellow per Krimmel); shawl white or blue; bonnet white cotton or straw; laundress petticoat striped or plain homespun (pink-stripe, blue, brown), apron white or checked, head handkerchief blue cotton.
build.fit: Gown waist high under bust, skirt narrow in front, ankle length; sleeves long and close or short puffed with long gloves. Short gown loose to the hip, worn over a petticoat to the ankle or just above.

references.evidences: Chicago, August 1812: Mrs. Heald's bonnet; plundered 'shawls, ribbons, and feathers' and 'a muslin gown, and the bonnet of one of the ladies'; Mrs. Helm disguised in 'the ordinary dress of a French woman of the country; namely, a short gown and petticoat, with a blue cotton handkerchief wrapped around her head' (1856 ed., narrative of the massacre, pp. 233-236; IA waubunearlydayin00kinz_0). The existing record's locator does not cite these passages

roles.role: Prosperous trader / merchant about 1810 (John Kinzie) and his wife (Eleanor Kinzie)

garments: Man: dark wool tailcoat (blue, green, brown or black), double- or single-breasted, cut square or cut away at the waist, tails to the knee, high turned collar; waistcoat (white, buff, yellow or a coloured silk), standing collar; white shirt with frill and a white neckcloth tied high; knee breeches with buttoned knee bands (older man of 49) or pantaloons/trousers; stockings and shoes, or top boots for riding; tall round hat with a moderate brim. roles.role: French Canadian / Métis engagés and voyageurs, and a Métis or French woman of the country

garments: Engagé/voyageur in August: shirt (often coloured/printed calico; Wau-Bun's 1830 traders wear 'calico shirts'), trousers or breechcloth with leggings, moccasins, a red knitted cap ('bonnet rouge, or tuque as the voyageurs call it'), a beaded worsted arrow sash at the waist; a hooded capot of grey (or blue/white blanket) cloth carried or worn in cool weather. Grades: issue of blanket, shirt, trousers direct (Heriot 1807); habitant capot, sash, moccasins, red cap direct (Lambert 1810, Lower Canada); tuque name direct (Wau-Bun, 1830, Fox River); breechcloth and leggings for paddlers: not evidenced in sources opened here (reconstruction; Native dress is another researcher's scope).
Summer substitution: 'the long coat is exchanged for a jacket, and the bonnet rouge for a straw hat' (Lambert): direct.
Hair: long queue tied behind (Lambert) for habitants: direct for Lower Canada.
Sash: finger-woven wool with glass beads, about 11 cm wide and nearly 3 m long (McCord M8486, about 1800); colours not seen: reconstruct red/blue/green/yellow chevrons and record the liberty.

Woman of the country (French or Métis): short gown and petticoat, a blue cotton handkerchief tied round the head (Wau-Bun, Chicago 1812, direct); apron, kerchief; moccasins likely (Lambert: moccasins 'in general use among the country people'): inferred.
build.colours: capot dark grey (Lambert) or blanket white/blue; cap red; sash multicoloured with red dominant (reconstructed); shirt printed/blue/white calico; trousers blue or natural linen; moccasins tan smoked leather; woman's head handkerchief blue cotton, short gown printed cotton, petticoat dark homespun.
build.fit: Capot loose, knee or thigh length, hooded, belted by the sash; trousers loose.

roles.role: Black servant or enslaved person in the Old Northwest about 1810

garments: Evidence of dress in the region and period is THIN: no picture or description of a Black person's clothing at Chicago, Detroit, Vincennes or St. Louis about 1810 was found in this pass.
Presence is recorded: Wau-Bun names 'Black Jim, one of the servants' in the Kinzie family's boat on 15 August 1812 (no dress recorded), and the household's nurse 'Grutte'.

What can be built, as reconstruction bounded by eastern evidence: a working man in shirt (white, red or checked), waistcoat, loose linen or wool trousers, round black hat or head-wrap, shoes or barefoot in summer (Krimmel's Black Sawyers, Philadelphia 1811-13); a working woman in head-wrap, short gown or bodice and petticoat, apron (same sheet). The Wau-Bun French woman's dress (short gown, petticoat, head handkerchief) is the best Chicago-1812 evidence for any working woman of the household.
Do not dress the figure in livery or in anything implying a status the record does not give; record the identity as reconstructed.
build.colours: as the working figures: white/red/checked shirt, striped or green waistcoat, blue or mustard trousers, black round hat; woman's head-wrap white or coloured, petticoat striped.

notes: All Met objects were checked in the Met collection API (isPublicDomain true) and every image named was downloaded and looked at on 2026-11-07; descriptions are what was seen, not catalogue text, except where the museum label is quoted. Every museum garment is a pattern for cut and cloth, not evidence of what anyone at Chicago wore. Strongest Chicago-specific evidence: Wau-Bun (1856; existing source kinzie_waubun_1856) for the women's bonnets, muslin gown, shawls, ribbons and feathers at the fort, the 'ordinary dress of a French woman of the country' (short gown, petticoat, blue cotton head-handkerchief), and Black Jim's presence. Recommend extending the existing records rather than duplicating them: met_krimmel_1813_philadelphia_soldiery (its access_notes miss the officer in chapeau, sash and boots and the drummer in a red coat faced blue); us_1814_military_laws_and_regulations (pp. 263-273 carry the staff/artillery/dragoon officer and NCO details used here by analogy, including surgeons' and mates' black velvet cape and black plume); kinzie_waubun_1856 (locator should add the 1812 narrative and the p. 44 tuque). Gaps and leads not verified: (1) H. A. Ogden plate XII, 'General, staff, infantry 1810-1813' (1888; a later reconstruction like the existing plate XI) is the natural companion to loc_ogden_1888_infantry_artillery_1802_1810, but loc.gov was blocked by a bot check this session and the item was not opened. (2) The 30 December 1812 Adjutant General's description is known here only through a reenactor page with no archival citation; find it in the War Department letters (National Archives RG 107 / RG 92) or a printed edition before relying on it. (3) No infantry-specific primary text for 1812 sergeants' or corporals' marks or musicians' coats was found; the NCO epaulettes come from the 1814 light dragoon text and the red musician's coat from Krimmel's volunteer drummer. (4) No fatigue-cap evidence for 1812; the issue has a frock and trousers only. (5) No portrait of Nathan or Rebekah Heald, Linai or Margaret Helm, John or Eleanor Kinzie, or Isaac Van Voorhis was found. (6) Runaway advertisements in the Missouri Gazette (St. Louis, 1808-) or Vincennes Western Sun would be the regional evidence for Black and working dress about 1810; not searched successfully in this pass. (7) The McCord sash and the Rindisbacher canoe were not seen as images; colours are reconstruction. (8) Andrew Jackson's uniform coat (NMAH AF.16082, ca. 1812-13, CC0 per the Smithsonian open-access API) exists as a surviving 1812-era officer's coat, but no record page was opened; a general's coat in any case. Do not invent Native dress here; another researcher covers Potawatomi and Miami dress.
